content:
In #39026 I have a PR adding an assume tactic. assume p, q, r is equivalent to intro (_ : p) (_ : q) (_ : r).
I wrote this tactic, because I think it looks nice in a demo.
Example:

open Function
example {α β γ} {g : β → γ} {f : α → β} (hg : Injective g) (hf :  Injective f) :
    Injective (g ∘ f) := by
  intro x y
  assume g (f x) = g (f y)
  have : f x = f y := by grind
  show x = y
  grind

In Mathlib, it can be used for a proof style where you try to limit referring to explicit names of hypotheses and theorems (this is of course not always easy, but IMO gives nice proofs if it works - I believe @Heather Macbeth likes this style). The downside is that it gives a second way to write something we can already write easily.

Do we want to use this tactic in Mathlib?
If not: do we still want to have the tactic in Mathlib, maybe in e.g. a subfolder TeachingTactics (or Tactic.Teaching) that should not be imported in Mathlib itself? I think that could be useful for the discoverability of such tactics.
I think this would be a nice teaching tactic. I'd prefer not to use it in mathlib. It could be used in the Archive, if it's useful there.

I was giving a live demo in a talk yesterday, and with the goal \forall U : Set X, IsOpen U -> blah I wrote

-- now assume U is an open subset of X
intro U hU

whereas with this tactic I could have written

-- now assume U is an open subset of X
intro U
assume IsOpen U

which is probably better, although I want to use the name of the hypothesis later on so

assume hU : IsOpen U

would be nicer for me I guess.

I guess the counterargument is "we don't want lots of tactics which basically do the same thing", an argument which appeals to some people (but not to me particularly).

assume hU : IsOpen U

would duplicate intro. Whether it's worth having this separate name is a different question, but I'd tend to say "not in mathlib".

You can do intro (hU : IsOpen U) already, by the way.
edit: fixed syntax
Maybe we could even make it that you can write assume IsOpen U without the previous intro U line?
but without intro U, then the Set X is not bound to a name?

Kevin Buzzard said:

I was giving a live demo in a talk yesterday, and with the goal \forall U : Set X, IsOpen U -> blah I wrote

-- now assume U is an open subset of X
intro U hU

whereas with this tactic I could have written

-- now assume U is an open subset of X
intro U
assume IsOpen U

which is probably better, although I want to use the name of the hypothesis later on so

assume hU : IsOpen U

would be nicer for me I guess.

The syntax I use in How To Prove It with Lean is

fix U : Set X
assume hU : IsOpen U

My fix tactic also checks to make sure that the goal is a "for all" statement, and gives an error if not. Similarly, assume checks to make sure that the goal is an implication, and gives an error if not. There's no reason for such checks in Mathlib, but for teaching I think they are helpful.
Which of fix or assume is allowed for \forall (h : m = n), Fin.cast h 0 = 0?

fix.
Determining whether an expression is universally quantified or an implication is tricky, because both are represented using Expr.forallE. The test I use is: if either the forallE is dependent or the domain is not a proposition, then it is universally quantified; otherwise, it is an implication. In the case of your example, it is dependent, so it is universally quantified.

I think this is the test that is used by the pretty printer, as implemented by #7812. So the use of fix or assume matches the pretty printing of the goal.

Of course, this issue doesn't come up in How To Prove It with Lean, in which quantification over proofs of propositions never occurs.
I think there's some consensus for change being code smell, and given that assume is intro + change I think the same principle applies.

There's quite a difference between code written for a library and code written for pedagogical purposes (the fact that mathlib is unreadable to mathematicians who are lean beginners is evidence for this claim) and ideas about what counts as a code smell for one domain don't necessarily transfer to the other. The clear proof I gave in my demo that the composite of two continuous functions was continuous can be golfed to hell, for example, thus rendering it unreadable.
I'm trying to answer the "do we want to use this in Mathlib" question. As a didactic tool I think this might be helpful.

Violeta Hernández said:

I think there's some consensus for change being code smell, and given that assume is intro + change I think the same principle applies.

In my version of assume, assume p, has the same behavior as intro (_ : p) for propositions p.
intro is already able to change the statement of a hypothesis. As you said, this is definitely desirable in demos, but might be undesirable in Mathlib.

I was first sceptical because for me it's indeed compelling not to introduce new tactics doing the same as existing ones (intro). However, I've now spent a moment looking at #39026 and now I think this a nice tool worth having, so I've reviewed the PR (leaving it at awaiting-zulip).

I don't have an opinion whether any style guide should discourage its usage. People here seem to prefer that, so we should probably start with that.

As for a bit more structure inside Mathlib.Tactic, I think that would be a good idea. Mathlib's have syntax without := is one example that could be in the same group. (but that's probably almost a new topic)

As a data point, let me point out that this tactic obviously exists in Verbose Lean and in Rocq waterproof (which are both teaching libraries). However I’m not sure we want that in Mathlib if its use is forbidden there.
